author: Sapnken, Kibong, et al.

steps.title: Define variables and sequences
steps.instruction: Assume that a system has N variables (or sequences) defined as follows:(1)X(0)={X1(0);X2(0),…,XN(0)}where X1(0) represents the dependant variable. There are N−1 inputs in the system defined by Xi(0)(i=2,...,N) which represent explanatory variables (or independent variables). X1(0) and Xi(0)(i=2,...,N) are strongly correlated with each other. We also assume that the sequence length for each variable Xi(0)(i=1,...,N) is n, so:(2)Xi(0)={xi(0)(1),xi(0)(2),…,xi(0)(n)},i=1,2,…,N.

steps.title: Defects of GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Definition 1Let's consider the independent and dependant variable sequences to be Xi(0)(i=2,...,N) and X1(0) respectively. With Xi(1)(i=1,...,N) as defined in Eq. (3), the GMC(1,N) model is then given by Eq. (5):(5)dx1(1)(t)dt+αx1(1)(t)=u+∑i=2Nβixi(1)(t)where u is the model parameter, ∑i=2Nβixi(1)(t) and βi are the deriving term and deriving coefficients respectively, while −α is referred to as the system development coefficient.

steps.title: Defects of GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: The differential equation (DE) model family includes GMC(1,N) as shown in Definition 1. The right-hand side (RHS) of Eq. (5) is generally not a constant, in contrast to the conventional GM(1,1). As a result, the GMC(1,N) model's time response function1 or solution to Eq. (5) is substantially more complicated than that of the GM(1,1) model. Ref. [4] first approximates Eq. (5) as a difference equation (Eq. (6b)) by considering the RHS of Eq. (5) to be a function f(t) as in Eq. (6a):(6a)u+∑i=2Nβixi(1)(t)=f(t)(6b)x1(0)(t)+αz1(1)(t)=u+∑i=2Nβizi(1)(t),t=2,…,n

steps.instruction: Eq. (6b) is obtained by integrating Eq. (5) on either sides in the range [t−1,t] and then applying the trapezoidal integration rule to the remaining unknown terms. In light of the parameters A=[α,β2,...,βN,u]T, the difference equation (Eq. (6b)) is a set of linear equations. Specifically:(7)BA=Ywhere:(8){B=(−z1(1)(2)z2(1)(2)…zN(1)(2)1−z1(1)(3)z2(1)(3)…zN(1)(3)1⋮⋮⋱⋮⋮−z1(1)(n)z2(1)(n)…zN(1)(n)1)∈R(n−1)×(N+1)Y=(x1(0)(2)x1(0)(3)⋮x1(0)(n))∈R(n−1)×1

steps.title: Defects of GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Going further, Tien [4] solved the DE given in Eq. (5) using the initial condition (when t=1) x^1(1)(1)=x1(0)(1), and obtained:(10)x^1(1)(t)=x1(0)(1)eα(1−t)+∫τ=1τ=teα(τ−t)f(τ)dτ

steps.instruction: Eq. (10) is known as the cumulated forecast function of GMC(1,N). Ref. [4] provides a thorough explanation of how the solution was derived. However, it is still challenging to obtain an explicit expression because the convolution integral exists on the RHS of Eq. (10). Fortunately, we can get a rough solution by using some numerical integrals. The trapezoid formula is a straightforward and widely used technique that yields a more precise time response function shown below2:(11)x^1(1)(t)=x1(0)(1)eα(1−t)+0.5h(t)∑τ=2t(f(τ)eα(τ−t)+f(τ−1)eα(τ−t−1));t≥2

steps.title: Defects of GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: It is important to highlight that GMC(1,N) is an evolution of both the conventional GM(1,1) and GM(1,N) models. Also, we make the following key remarks:

steps.title: Defects of GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Remark. 1The second term in the RHS of Eq. (5) disappears if there is only one series (N=1, and is known as a univariate model) and the model is reduced to:dx1(1)(t)dt+αx1(1)(t)=u,

steps.title: Calculate GM(1,1) model parameters
steps.instruction: This DE is the GM(1,1) model's traditional image equation. From Eq. (10), we obtain the following by setting f(τ) equal to a fixed value u:x1(1)(1)=x1(0)(1)eα(1−t)+∫τ=1τ=teα(τ−t)udτ=x1(0)(1)eα(1−t)+uα(eαt−eα)e−αt=uα+(x1(0)−uα)eα(1−t)which is the GM(1,1) model's time response function. The least-squares method of Eq. (7) can still be used to solve the parameters u and α. Except that B is reduced to:(12)B=(−z1(0)(2)1−z1(0)(3)1⋮⋮−z1(0)(n)1)∈R(n−1)×2

substeps.instruction: Set f(τ) equal to a fixed value u
Use x1(1)(1) = x1(0)(1)eα(1−t) + ∫τ=1τ=teα(τ−t)udτ
Substitute to obtain x1(1)(1) = x1(0)(1)eα(1−t) + uα(eαt−eα)e−αt
Rearrange to get x1(1)(1) = uα + (x1(0)−uα)eα(1−t)
Apply least-squares method from Eq. (7) to solve for u and α
Note that B is reduced to B = (−z1(0)(2)1−z1(0)(3)1⋮⋮−z1(0)(n)1)∈R(n−1)×2

steps.title: Defects of GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Remark 2GMC(1,N) provided by Eq. (5) reduces to Eq. (13) if u=0.(13)dx1(1)(t)dt+αx1(1)(t)=∑i=2Nβixi(1)(t)

steps.title: Defects of GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Eq. (13) is the GM(1,N) model's standard image equation. The RHS of Eq. (13) is viewed as a constant in the pioneers’ works (see Ref. [5]). As a result, the cumulated forecast function of GM(1,N) may be derived exactly as that of the conventional GM(1,1):x^1(1)(1)=(x1(0)(t)−1α∑i=2Nβixi(1)(t))eα(t−1)+1α∑i=2Nβixi(1)(t).

steps.title: Defects of GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Compared to GMC(1,N), GM(1,N) contains one fewer parameter in the matrix A˜=[α,β2,...,βN]T. The least-squares technique can also be used to calculate the values of these parameters. B also shows a difference, which is:B=(−z1(1)(2)x2(1)(2)…xN(1)(2)−z1(1)(3)x2(1)(3)…xN(1)(3)⋮⋮⋱⋮−z1(1)(n)x2(1)(n)…xN(1)(n))∈R(n−1)×N

steps.title: Defects of GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Based on Remarks 1 and 2, it is obvious that GMC(1,N) is theoretically better than the classical GM(1,N) in three following aspects:(i)In contrast to the GMC(1,N) model's structure, the conventional GM(1,N) cannot be transformed to GM(1,1).(ii)The driving term ∑i=2Nβixi(1)(t) depends on t in GMC(1,N), yet this term is viewed as being fixed in the classical GM(1,N), which is obviously incorrect. Consequently, the cumulated forecast function of GM(1,N) is also incorrect.(iii)GM(1,N) makes better sense when computing the parameters A=[α,β2,...,βN,u]T. The second to Nth column of B stems from integration in GMC(1,N), but in the conventional GM(1,N), they are treated as constants.

steps.title: Defects of GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Even so, GMC(1,N) remains flawed in three respects:(i)Parameterization mismatch: The least squares method is used to solve the difference equation in Eq. (6b) in order to estimate A=[α,β2,...,βN,u]T from GMC(1,N). However, the first-order DE provided in Eq. (10) is used to create the time response function (see Eq (5)). Although the DE and the difference equation in Eq. (6b) approximate each other, they are fundamentally distinct. GMC(1,N) may become unstable as a result of this discrepancy in the estimation and application of the parameters.(ii)Structural defects: GMC(1,N) is a causal model just like the conventional GM(1,N) [4], and therefore relies on various system factors. There are still some issues with structural rigidity in GMC(1,N). Though, its structure has undergone many modifications, most works have failed to address the linear impact of t on GMC(1,N)’s behaviour, which could explain why the model's predictive accuracy is poor.(iii)Presence of noise in data: Finally, most studies have not taken into account the possibility that the input data may contain irrelevant information, which could also reduce the model's ability to predict outcomes accurately.

steps.title: Develop improved GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: In view of the previous analysis, it follows that GMC(1,N) remains flawed due to inadequate parameter estimation and its structure is too simple to cope with real-world systems. These obvious defects urges us to develop a GMC(1,N) that overcomes them.

steps.title: The proposed optimal model
steps.instruction: We briefly discussed the GMC(1,N) model in Section 2.1 and demonstrated that it is in fact an upgrade of the conventional GM(1,N). It suffers from several glaring flaws, though. In this section, a novel optimal discrete multivariate GMC model (abbreviated ODGMC(1,N)) is developed as a solution to these flaws, enhancing the precision and stability of the GMC(1,N) model while also addressing their causes.

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: We start by introducing a new definition that is based on the concept examined by Ref. [6].

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Definition 2Let Eqs. (1) and (2) still serve as the definitions for X1(0) and X1(0),(i=2,3,...,N). Then, considering the 1-AGO sequences Xi(1),(i=1,2,...,N) as in Eq (3). So:(14)dx1(1)(t)dt+αx1(1)(t)=∑i=2Nβixi(1)(t)+(t−1)λ1+λ2

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Eq. (14) is known as the optimized GMC(1,N) model's image equation. The system's development coefficient is −α, the system's driving term is ∑i=2Nβixi(1)(t) with driving coefficients βi, whereas (t−1)λ1 and λ2 respectively represent the linear correction and model's parameter.

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: To improve the structure of GMC(1,N) in comparison, an additional linear adjustment term (t−1)λ1 has been added in the RHS of Eq. (5). Many works on grey multivariate models (for example: Zeng et al. [[6], [7]]) have come to the conclusion that this linear adjustment factor is crucial and can easily change the degree to which X1(0) and X1(0),(i=2,3,...,N) are related. However, in these earlier studies, the DE is not used; instead, the linear correction factor is included right into the difference equation. Moreover, if we apply the same methodology used to derive the cumulated forecast function of GMC(1,N), we get an expression similar to Eq. (10), with the exception that f(τ) becomes:f(τ)=∑i=2Nβixi(1)(t)+(t−1)λ1+λ2

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: As a result, the parameter estimation mismatch flaw mentioned in Section 2.1 continues to exist. Fortunately, this mismatch issue can be eliminated by employing the discrete grey model methodology.

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: The novel ODGMC(1,N) outlined in the next subsections, is founded on optimized GMC(1,N) model's image equation described in Definition 2. When we integrate both sides of Eq. (14) in the range [k,k+1], we get:(15)∫kk+1dx1(1)(t)+∫kk+1αx1(1)(t)dt=∑i=2Nβi∫kk+1xi(1)(t)dt+∫kk+1(t−1)λ1dt+∫kk+1λ2dt

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: By recalling that: x1(1)(k+1)−x1(1)(k)=x1(0)(k+1), Eq. (15) can be written as:x1(0)(k+1)+α∫kk+1x1(1)(t)dt=∑i=2Nβi∫kk+1xi(1)(t)dt+(k−12)λ1+λ2

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: In order to integrate the undefined functions, we can use the trapezoidal formula as follows:(16)∫kk+1xi(1)(t)dt=(xi(1)(k+1)+xi(1)(k))2Δ=zi(1)(k+1)

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Applying this formula to both unknown terms in Eq. (15), we get:(17)x1(0)(k+1)+αz1(1)(k+1)=∑i=2Nβizi(1)(k+1)+(k−12)λ1+λ2

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Substituting Eq. (18) into Eq. (17) and simplifying, we have:(19)x1(1)(k+1)=φ1x1(1)(k)+∑i=2Nφizi(1)(k+1)+μ1k+μ2where: φ1=(1−α2)(1+α2); φi=βi(1+α2),(i=2,3,…,N); μ1=λ1(1+α2); μ2=λ2−λ12(1+α2)

steps.title: ODGMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: Eq. (19) is then called the optimised discrete multivariate GMC model.

steps.title: Parameterization of the optimised discrete GMC(1,N) model
steps.instruction: From Eq. (19), it comes out that N+2 parameters given by the matrix A=[φ1,φ2,...,φN,μ1,μ2]T need to be obtained by finding the solution of the linear set of equations in Eq. (20):(20)BA=Ywhere,(21){B=(x1(1)(1)z2(1)(2)…zN(1)(2)11x1(1)(2)z2(1)(3)…zN(1)(3)21⋮⋮⋱⋮⋮⋮x1(1)(n−1)z2(1)(n)…zN(1)(n)n−11)∈R(n−1)×(N+2)Y=(x1(1)(2)x1(1)(3)⋮x1(1)(n))∈R(n−1)×1

steps.title: Evaluation of the predicted accumulated and original series
steps.instruction: The following theorem describes the application of the recursive technique (similar to that of discrete grey models [8,9]) in order to determine the ODGMC(1,N) model's cumulated forecast function:

steps.title: Evaluation of the predicted accumulated and original series
steps.instruction: Theorem: The cumulated forecast function of ODGMC(1,N), as specified in Eq. (19), is as follows under the initial condition x^1(1)(t=1)=x1(0)(1):(22)x^1(1)(t+1)=φ1tx1(0)(t)+∑j=1tφ1t−j(∑i=2Nφizi(1)(j+1)+μ1j+μ2),t≥1

steps.title: Evaluation of the predicted accumulated and original series
steps.instruction: The appendix shows the proof. This Theorem demonstrates that Eq. (22) can be used to evaluate the 1-AGO series x^1(1). As a result, the inverse-AGO can be used to determine the forecasted series x^1(0) as follows:x^1(0)(t+1)=x^1(1)(t+1)−x^1(1)(t),t≥1

steps.title: Data filtration based on wavelet transform
steps.instruction:
ODGMC(1,N) may be corrupted by noise or useless information in the raw data. Wavelet transform (WT) can be used to clean this noise [10]. A wavelet is a mathematical function that separates various scale components from a continuous-time signal. Basically, WT is a band-pass filter with its bandwidth scaled to half at each level [11]. The scaling function makes sure that the entire spectrum is considered by filtering away the transform's lowest level. Eq. (23) applies when a signal x(t) is continuous:(23)CWTΨ(η,ϑ)=1|η|∫−∞+∞x(t)Ψ*(t−ϑη)dtwhere the scale and translation parameters, are denoted by η and ϑ
(η,ϑ∈R) respectively. Eq. (23) is called the continuous wavelet transform (CWT).

steps.title: Calculate discrete WT using Eq. (24)
steps.instruction: With a discrete signal xj, a discrete WT (DWT) is calculated using Eq. (24):(24)DWTx(p,q)=12p∑jxjΨ*(j−q2p)where q=1,2,…N and p are the sampling time and scale factor respectively. N is the number of samples. The most crucial element of the signal is its low order component. The signal's identity is clarified in this component. The signal's high order component, on the other hand, is a representation of the signal's specifics.

substeps.instruction: Use p as the sampling time and scale factor
Calculate DWTx(p,q) = 1/(2p) * ΣjxjΨ*(j−q/(2p))

steps.title: Data selection
steps.instruction: Data used in this method paper cover the period 2000–2019 and were collected from IEA and World Bank's development indicators (WDI). Specifically, dataset on electricity consumption is from IEA (https://www.iea.org/). In contrast, datasets on GDP per capita, household expenses and population size come from WDI (https://databank.worldbank.org) and are confirmed by the National Institute of Statistics (https://ins-cameroun.cm/).

steps.title: Performance evaluation
steps.instruction: The reliability and forecast precision are evaluated using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Square Error (MSE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) and Absolute Percentage Error (APE).

steps.title: Performance evaluation
steps.instruction: MAPE and APE disclose the models’ predictive accuracy. MAPE in particular is a performance metric that compares the accuracy of forecasts based on relative errors to prevent positive and negative errors from mutually annulling. Threshold values of MAPE are given in Table 1. The formulae for calculating APE and MAPE are defined by Eqs. (25) and (26):(25)APE=|x^1(0)(t)−x1(0)(t)x1(0)(t)|×100%(26)MAPE=1Ns∑t=1Ns|x^1(0)(t)−x1(0)(t)x1(0)(t)|×100%Table 1Thresholds for MAPE [12].Table 1MAPE(%)Accuracy levelMAPE(%)Accuracy level]0;5]Class I: Extremely high precision]10;20]Class III: Average precision]5;10]Class II: Good precision]20;+∞[Class IV: Low precision

steps.title: Calculate Mean Squared Error (MSE)
steps.instruction: MSE (defined in Eq. (27)) is very often considered as a loss function. It is calculated by adding the square of the difference between real x1(0)(t) and forecasted electricity consumption x^1(0)(t), over all the data points and dividing the result by number of data points.(27)MSE=1Ns∑t=1Ns(x^1(0)(t)−x1(0)(t))2

substeps.instruction: Add the square of the difference between real x1(0)(t) and forecasted electricity consumption x^1(0)(t)
Sum the results over all data points
Divide the result by the number of data points Ns

steps.title: Performance evaluation
steps.instruction: RMSE (Eq. (28)) is the square root of MSE. RMSE acts much like the MSE except that it is prone to inflate significant deviations [13], and this may be useful when comparing competing models.(28)RMSE=MSE

steps.title: Evaluate model using RMSE MSE MAPE APE
steps.instruction: The best performing model in indicated by a score of RMSE, MSE, MAPE and APE that is closest to zero. However, we focus more on MAPE because it is a metric that comes up very often in forecasting studies. MAPE is usually expressed as a percentage error making it easy to grasp and compare the accuracy of a model across data sets and case studies.

steps.title: Analyze GM(1,N) predictions
steps.instruction: GM(1,N) predictions (yellow curve) fit moderately well in the modelling phase (Table 2) but completely deviates in the validation phase, meaning it is overfitting. Of all alternative models, only the GMC(1,N) manages to compete with the new ODGMC(1,N) model. It can be seen from Fig. 1 that the new ODGMC(1,N) manages to correctly track the system's evolution in both the modelling and validation phases.

steps.title: Forecasting annual electricity consumption
steps.instruction: APE distribution (see Fig. 2) for the training and validation phases shows that the residuals of ODGMC(1,N) model are much more smaller than those of GM(1,1), GM(1,N) and GMC(1,N). So, this also reiterates the superiority of ODGMC(1,N) model. MAPE criteria in particular, with statistics of 2.74% and 1.99% in the modelling and validation phase respectively, demonstrates that ODGMC(1,N) is a class I model and can compete with high accuracy models.Fig. 2APE distribution of simulations.Fig 2

steps.title: Appendix. Proof of theorem leading to Eq. (22)
steps.instruction: Proof: Let ∑i=2Nφizi(1)(t+1)+μ1t+μ2=w(t) be an auxiliary function (that we introduce for convenience).

steps.title: Appendix. Proof of theorem leading to Eq. (22)
steps.instruction: According to Eq. (19), the cumulated forecast function of ODGMC(1,N) can be determine as follows:x^1(1)(t+1)=φ1x^1(1)(t)+w(t)=φ1(φ1x^1(1)(t−1)+w(t−1))+w(t)=φ12x^1(1)(t−1)+φ1w(t−1)+w(t)=⋯=φ1tx^1(1)(1)+φ1t−1w(1)+φ1t−2w(2)+⋯+φ1w(t−1)+w(t)

steps.title: Appendix. Proof of theorem leading to Eq. (22)
steps.instruction: Under the initial condition x^1(1)(t=1)=x1(0)(1), we have:x^1(1)(t+1)=φ1tx1(0)(t)+∑j=1tw(j)φ1t−j.

steps.title: Appendix. Proof of theorem leading to Eq. (22)
steps.instruction: Substituting ∑i=2Nφizi(1)(t+1)+μ1t+μ2=w(t) in the previous expression immediately results in the given time response function defined by Eq. (22). This completes the proof.
